Lesson 1.4 · 15 min · Verified 17 Jul 2026

From circular to control: how LoanOS encodes regulation

After this lesson you can:
  • Explain 'compliance evidence produced while the business flow runs'
  • Distinguish fail-closed controls from after-the-fact checklists
  • Read a capability status honestly (Implemented / Partial / Mock)
On this page
  1. The core design bet
  2. Fail closed, by default
  3. Honest maturity language
  4. Where this lives in LoanOS
  5. Knowledge check

1. The core design bet

Most lending stacks bolt compliance on afterwards: the business flow runs, and a reporting team reconstructs evidence when the auditor calls.

LoanOS inverts this — compliance evidence is produced while the business flow runs.

The KFS is not a PDF someone remembered to attach; it is a data object that gates sanction.

Consent is not a checkbox log; it is a ledger the application preflight reads.

A missing control does not produce a warning; it produces a blocked transition.

For a BA this changes how you write requirements: a regulatory obligation is done only when the flow cannot proceed without producing its evidence.

2. Fail closed, by default

The platform's non-negotiable rule is fail closed: when a check cannot be evaluated — service down, evidence missing, policy expired — the outcome is the restrictive one (refer or deny), never a permissive default. An unavailable KYC provider does not mean 'skip KYC'; an unreachable decision engine does not mean 'approve'.

This matters to BAs because edge cases are where compliance usually leaks. When you specify a flow, always specify the failure path — LoanOS's answer is predetermined: land on the safe side and route to a human queue.

3. Honest maturity language

The capability catalogue classifies every capability as Implemented, Partial, Mock or Planned, and the journey support matrix assigns evidence tiers per lending journey.

The GTM glossary even bans phrases like 'RBI certified' and 'guaranteed compliant'.

This course inherits that discipline: a lesson explaining a process cites capability IDs, and the catalogue row — not the lesson — tells you how much is real today.

When you brief stakeholders, quote the status, never the aspiration.

Regulatory anchors

  • RBI-IT-GRC — IT governance directions demand controls, audit trails and straight-through-processing checks — the regulatory basis for controls-as-code.
  • RBI-KFS-2024 — Example of a rule that became a gate: KFS validation blocks decisioning and sanction.

Family IDs resolve in the India regulatory register (docs/compliance/india-regulatory-register.md), which owns sources and caveats.

Where this lives in LoanOS

  • Document docs/product/complete-system-capability-catalog.md — Capability register with Implemented/Partial/Mock status — the source of maturity truth.
  • Document docs/product/product-journey-support-matrix.md — Evidence tier for each lending journey; a guide existing is not production readiness.
  • Code packages/core/src/compliance/compliance-controls.js — The executable control catalogue: application preflight checks that fail closed.

Knowledge check

1. The KYC verification service is unreachable during an application. What does a fail-closed design do?

  1. Approve and verify later
  2. Proceed with a warning banner
  3. Block the transition and route to the restrictive path
  4. Retry silently forever
Show answer

C. Error paths land on the restrictive outcome — the application waits or refers; it never advances on missing evidence.

2. A stakeholder asks whether collections field receipts are production-ready. What is the BA's correct move?

  1. Say yes — there's a lesson about it
  2. Check the capability catalogue status and quote it
  3. Say no to be safe
  4. Ask engineering informally
Show answer

B. Maturity truth lives in the catalogue (e.g. CLL rows) and the journey support matrix; course content deliberately defers to them.
